{{Short description|American theoretical physicist}}
'''John Pascal Vinti''' (January 16, 1907, [[Newport, Rhode Island]]<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XQva31VXZeUC&q=vinti | isbn=9780835210171 | title=American Men and Women of Science | year=1977 | page=878 | publisher=R. R. Bowker LLC }}</ref> – September 28, 1990, Boston) was an American theoretical physicist, who published papers not only in physics, but also in mathematics and engineering.<ref name=obitPT>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.2809675|title=John P. Vinti |year=1992 |last1=Bonavito |first1=Nino L. |last2=Dressler |first2=Robert F. |last3=Garfinkle |first3=Boris |last4=Hollister |first4=Walter M. |last5=Janiczek |first5=Paul M. |journal=Physics Today |volume=45 |issue=5 |pages=77–78 |bibcode=1992PhT....45e..77B }}</ref> He is known for the Vinti integral.<ref>{{cite arxiv|eprint=1806.04547|last1=Kopeikin |first1=Sergei M. |author-link=Sergei Kopeikin|title=Carter-like Constant of Motion in Newtonian Gravity is the Vinti Integral |year=2018|class=gr-qc }}</ref>

==Biography==
His father, Giovanni Giuseppe Vinti (1885–1959), was born in [[Naples]], Italy. In 1922 John P. Vinti graduated from [[Rogers High School (Rhode Island)|Rogers High School]] in Newport, Rhode Island. At his high school graduation, he was honored with a prize in scholarship and a prize in mathematics.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R0EwAQAAMAAJ&q=vinti| title=Annual Report of the Public School Department of the City of Newport, Rhode Island 1922–1923| year=1918| volume=LVIII | publisher=Mercury Publishing Company }}</ref> At age 15 Vinti matriculated at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). There he graduated with a bachelor's degree in mathematics in 1927 and a Ph.D. in physics in 1932.<ref name=obitPT/> His thesis Ph.D. thesis is entitled ''Variational calculation of atomic wave functions''.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=d3suAAAAIAAJ&q=vinti&pg=PA45| page=45 | title=Doctorates Conferred in the Sciences by American Universities 1931–1932 | year=1932 |location=Washington, D.C. |publisher=National Research Council (U.S.) Research Information Service }}</ref> As a postdoc he worked at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] from 1932 to 1934 on helium's absorption spectrum.<ref name=obitPT/> He was from 1934 to 1935 an assistant at MIT, from 1936 to 1937 an instructor at [[Brown University]], from 1937 to 1938 an assistant professor at [[The Citadel]], and from 1939 to 1941 an instructor at [[Worcester Polytechnic Institute]]. In 1941 he joined the physics staff of the [[Ballistics Research Laboratory]] at Maryland's [[Aberdeen Proving Ground]]. There he became chief of the Interior Ballistics Theory Section and a senior physicist (as of 1945).<ref>{{cite book|editor=Cattell, Jaques|title=American Men of Science: A Biographical Dictionary|page=2581|year=1949|publisher=The Science Press|location=Lancaster, Pennsylvania|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ea9CC4lCicQC&pg=PA2581}}</ref> At Aberdeen he developed a keen interest in [[celestial mechanics]] and "a close professional relationship with [[John von Neumann]] and [[Maria Goeppert-Mayer]]."<ref name=obitPT/>

Later in his career, Vinti taught and did research at MIT as a professor in the department of [[aeronautics]] and [[astronautics]] in the 1970s<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DJP3oUAEvykC&pg=PA58| title=An Annotated Bibliography of Sandia Laboratories Publications Related to Terradynamics | year=1974 | page=58 |publisher=Sandia Laboratories }}</ref> and 1980s.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1119/1.14775|title=Note on ''The axioms underlying Maxwell's electromagnetic equations'' &#91;G. B. Walker, Am. J. Phys. 53, 1169 (1985)&#93; |year=1986 |last1=Vinti |first1=John P. |last2=Montgomery |first2=D. J. X. |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=54 |issue=10 |page=872 |bibcode=1986AmJPh..54..872V }}</ref>

Lecture notes that Vinti used in a course that he taught in 1966 at the [[Catholic University of America]] and later at MIT were posthumously published in 1998 as the book ''Orbital and Celestial Mechanics'', edited by Gim J. Der and Nino L. Bonavito. According to Der and Bonavito, Vinti's spheroidal method was "many years ahead of its time" and "predicts position and velocity vectors for satellites and ballistic missiles almost as accurately as numerical integration."<ref>{{cite book|author=Vinti, John Pascal|editor=Der, Gim J.|editor2=Bonavito, Nino L.|chapter=Preface|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-dXzdYHvPgMC&pg=PR15| page=xv | isbn=9781600864292 | title=Orbital and Celestial Mechanics | year=1998 |volume=177|series=Progress in Aeronautics and Astronautics|publisher=American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics|location=Reston, Virginia}}</ref>

He was elected in 1936 a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1936&unit_id=&institution=Brown+University}} (search on year=1936 and institution=Brown University)</ref>

Upon his death, John P. Vinti was survived by his sisters, Helena (1908–1995) and Anna (1911–2001), and their children. His nephew Jack Edmonston was his executor and was entrusted with the publication of ''Orbital and Celestial Mechanics''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://jackedmonston.com/uncle-john-cantankerous-absent-minded-professor/|title=Uncle John, the cantankerous, absent-minded professor &#124; Jack Edmonston's Blog |date=8 August 2018 }}</ref>

John P. Vinti is a distant relative of Italian mathematician Calogero Vinti, who is memorialized by the [[Vinti Prize]].

John P. Vinti is buried in Newton Cemetery in [[Newton, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Newton Cemetery & Arboretum|url=https://www.newcemcorp.org}}</ref>
